chapter_text:
CHAPTER 6 — यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति (YADBHAVISYO VINASYATI)

परिचयः — Introduction

The phrase यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति (yad-bhavisyo vinasyati) means literally "the one (called) 'What-will-be' perishes." It is the punch-line of one of the most famous animal fables (पशु-कथा / नीति-कथा) of India — the story of the THREE FISHES (त्रयः मत्स्याः) — found in the great collections of practical wisdom, the पञ्चतन्त्रम् (Panchatantra) and the हितोपदेशः (Hitopadesha). These works were composed to teach नीति (right conduct and worldly wisdom) to the young through short, delightful tales in which birds, beasts and fish speak and act like people. This lesson (NIOS Secondary Sanskrit, Course 209) retells that story in simple Sanskrit prose with शब्दार्थ (word meanings) and an English translation, draws out its moral (सन्देशः), studies the famous framing verse, and uses the tale to learn a little grammar (व्याकरणम्).

The three fishes carry meaningful names that ARE the lesson. अनागतविधाता (Anagata-vidhata) means "one who makes arrangements for what has not yet come" — that is, one who plans ahead for the future (अनागत = not-yet-come, future; विधाता = arranger, planner). प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः (Pratyutpanna-mati) means "one whose intelligence (मति) springs up on the spot" — presence of mind, ready wit (प्रत्युत्पन्न = arisen at the present moment). यद्भविष्यः (Yad-bhavisya) means simply "What-will-be" — the fatalist who says "whatever is going to happen will happen" and therefore does nothing to save himself. As the story shows, foresight and presence of mind save the first two fishes, while blind fatalism destroys the third.

कथा — The Story (सरल-संस्कृत-गद्ये)

कस्मिंश्चित् जलाशये त्रयः मत्स्याः वसन्ति स्म। तेषां नामानि आसन् — अनागतविधाता, प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः, यद्भविष्यः च। ते त्रयः अपि परस्परं मित्राणि आसन्, किन्तु तेषां स्वभावाः भिन्नाः आसन्।

एकदा सायंकाले केचन धीवराः (मत्स्यजीविनः) तस्य जलाशयस्य तीरम् आगच्छन्। जले बहवः पीनाः मत्स्याः सन्ति इति दृष्ट्वा ते परस्परम् अवदन् — "अहो! अत्र बहवः मत्स्याः सन्ति। श्वः प्रातःकाले वयम् आगत्य जालेन एतान् सर्वान् ग्रहीष्यामः" इति निश्चित्य ते स्वगृहम् अगच्छन्।

धीवराणां तत् वचनम् अनागतविधाता अशृणोत्। सः अचिन्तयत् — "श्वः महान् अनर्थः आगमिष्यति। बुद्धिमता पुरुषेण आपदः आगमनात् पूर्वम् एव प्रतिकारः कर्तव्यः। अतः अद्य एव अहम् इदं स्थानं त्यक्त्वा अन्यत्र गच्छामि" इति। एवं विचिन्त्य सः तस्मिन् एव क्षणे जलमार्गेण (नदी-प्रणालिकया) अन्यत् क्षेमकरं सरः अगच्छत्। एषा अस्य दूरदर्शिता (foresight) आसीत्।

द्वितीयः मत्स्यः प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः अचिन्तयत् — "यदा आपत् वस्तुतः आगमिष्यति, तदा एव अहं यथोचितम् उपायं करिष्यामि। सम्प्रति गमनस्य आवश्यकता नास्ति" इति। सः तत्र एव अतिष्ठत्।

तृतीयः मत्स्यः यद्भविष्यः तु अहसत्, अवदत् च — "यद् भविष्यति तद् एव भविष्यति। भाग्यम् एव प्रबलम्। किमर्थं वृथा चिन्ता? पूर्वजाः अपि अत्र एव वसन्ति स्म। अहम् अपि अत्र एव स्थास्यामि" इति। सः निश्चिन्तः निर्उद्यमः च तत्र एव अवसत्।

श्वः प्रातः धीवराः पुनः आगत्य जलाशये जालम् अक्षिपन्। अनागतविधाता तु पूर्वम् एव प्रयातः आसीत्, अतः सः सुरक्षितः आसीत्। प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः जाले बद्धः अभवत्, किन्तु सः तत्क्षणम् एव उपायम् अचिन्तयत्। सः मृतवत् निश्चलः भूत्वा जलस्य उपरि प्लवते स्म (as if dead)। धीवराः "अयं मत्स्यः मृतः" इति मत्वा तं जालात् बहिः क्षिप्तवन्तः। तत्क्षणम् एव सः चपलतया पुनः जले प्रविश्य दूरम् अपलायत। एषा अस्य प्रत्युत्पन्ना मतिः (presence of mind) आसीत्।

यद्भविष्यः तु किमपि उपायम् न अकरोत्। सः जालेन गृहीतः, धीवरैः च सह अन्यैः मत्स्यैः बहिः आनीतः। भाग्ये विश्वस्य आलस्येन अकर्मण्यः सन् सः धीवरैः हतः। एवं यद्भविष्यः विनष्टः। "यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति" इति एतत् एव कथायाः सारः।

शब्दार्थः — Word Meanings

जलाशयः = lake, pond; मत्स्यः = fish; वसन्ति स्म = used to live; नामानि = names; स्वभावः = nature, temperament; भिन्नः = different; धीवरः = fisherman; तीरम् = bank, shore; पीनः = fat, plump; जालम् = net; श्वः = tomorrow; प्रातःकाले = in the morning; ग्रहीष्यामः = (we) will catch/seize; निश्चित्य = having decided; अशृणोत् = heard; अनर्थः = misfortune, calamity; आपद् = danger, calamity; प्रतिकारः = remedy, counter-measure; पूर्वम् = before; त्यक्त्वा = having left; जलमार्गेण = by the water-way; सरः = lake; दूरदर्शिता = foresight; उपायः = means, plan, device; अतिष्ठत् = remained, stayed; भाग्यम् = fate, destiny; प्रबलम् = strong, powerful; वृथा = in vain, uselessly; निश्चिन्तः = free of worry, care-free; अक्षिपन् = threw, cast; बद्धः = bound, caught; निश्चलः = motionless; मृतवत् = as if dead; प्लवते = floats; मत्वा = having thought; अपलायत = ran away, escaped; गृहीतः = seized, caught; हतः = killed; विनष्टः = destroyed, perished; सारः = essence, gist.

अनुवादः — English Translation (gist)

In a certain lake there lived three fishes, named Anagata-vidhata ("Fore-planner"), Pratyutpanna-mati ("Ready-wit") and Yad-bhavisya ("What-will-be"). They were friends, but their natures differed. One evening some fishermen came to the bank, saw many plump fish, and said, "Tomorrow morning we shall come and catch them all with our net," and went home. The fish Anagata-vidhata overheard them and thought, "A great danger will come tomorrow; a wise person removes a calamity before it arrives," and at once, by the water-channel, he swam away to another safe lake — this was his FORESIGHT. The second fish, Pratyutpanna-mati, decided, "When the danger actually comes, I shall act then," and stayed. The third, Yad-bhavisya, laughed and said, "Whatever will be, will be; fate is supreme; why worry in vain?" and stayed care-free and idle. Next morning the fishermen cast their net. Anagata-vidhata was already gone and safe. Pratyutpanna-mati was caught, but instantly thought of a device: he floated motionless as if dead; the fishermen threw the "dead" fish out, and he darted back into the water and escaped — this was his PRESENCE OF MIND. But Yad-bhavisya made no effort at all; trusting only to fate and lazy, he was caught and killed. Thus "Yad-bhavisya perishes" — that is the essence of the tale.

सन्देशः — The Moral

The story teaches नीति (practical wisdom) through contrast. दूरदर्शिता (foresight) — thinking ahead and acting before trouble strikes — keeps Anagata-vidhata completely safe. प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः (presence of mind) — the ability to think of a clever device at the very moment of crisis — saves Pratyutpanna-mati even after he is caught. But अन्ध-भाग्यवादः / दैववादः (blind fatalism) — leaving everything to fate and making no effort (पुरुषार्थ) oneself — destroys Yad-bhavisya. The lesson is NOT that fate does not exist, but that a wise person combines effort with intelligence: one should plan for the future, keep a cool and ready mind in danger, and never use "whatever will be, will be" as an excuse for laziness (आलस्य) and inaction.

श्लोकः — The Framing Verse (सुभाषितम्, public domain)

अनागतविधाता च प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिस्तथा ।
द्वावेतौ सुखमेधेते यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति ॥

शब्दार्थः: अनागतविधाता = the fore-planner (one who plans for the future); च = and; प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः = the ready-witted one (presence of mind); तथा = likewise, and so; द्वौ = the two; एतौ = these; सुखम् = happily, in comfort; एधेते = thrive, prosper (dual, from धातु √एध् 'to grow/thrive'); यद्भविष्यः = "What-will-be", the fatalist; विनश्यति = perishes, is destroyed.

अन्वयार्थः (meaning): "Anagata-vidhata (the fore-planner) and, likewise, Pratyutpanna-mati (the ready-witted) — these two thrive happily; but Yad-bhavisya (the fatalist) perishes." The verse names all three fishes and states the whole moral in a single line: foresight and presence of mind lead to well-being; blind fatalism leads to ruin.

व्याकरणम् — Grammar from the Lesson

(A) सन्धि (euphonic combination). When sounds meet they often merge and change; splitting them back is सन्धि-विच्छेद.
  • यण्-सन्धि: प्रति + उत्पन्नः = प्रत्युत्पन्नः. Here इ (of प्रति) before the dissimilar vowel उ becomes the semivowel य्, giving प्रत्य्-उत्पन्न → प्रत्युत्पन्न.
  • नञ्/दीर्घ-सन्धि: न (नञ्, 'not') + आगतः → अनागतः ('not come' = future). The negative नञ् appears as अन् before a vowel; अन् + आगत = अनागत.
  • व्यञ्जन-सन्धि: यद् + भविष्यः = यद्भविष्यः (the द् stays before भ). सुखम् + एधेते = सुखमेधेते (म् joins the following vowel).
  • विसर्ग/other: कः + चित् forms like कस्मिंश्चित् (कस्मिन् + चित्) show consonant sandhi at word-joins.

(B) विभक्ति (case endings) — using the a-stem मत्स्य ('fish') and words from the story:
  • प्रथमा (nominative, subject): मत्स्यः 'the fish', धीवराः 'the fishermen' (plural), त्रयः मत्स्याः 'three fishes'.
  • द्वितीया (accusative, object): मत्स्यम् 'the fish (as object)', मत्स्यान् 'the fishes' (plural) — 'they will catch the FISHES'.
  • तृतीया (instrumental, 'by/with'): जालेन 'by the net', धीवरैः 'by the fishermen', जलमार्गेण 'by the water-way'.
  • पञ्चमी (ablative, 'from'): आगमनात् 'from (before) the arriving', जालात् 'from the net'.
  • षष्ठी (genitive, 'of'): जलाशयस्य 'of the lake', धीवराणाम् 'of the fishermen'.
  • सप्तमी (locative, 'in/at'): जलाशये 'in the lake', जले 'in the water', तीरे 'on the bank'.

(C) शब्दरूप — declension of मत्स्य (masc., a-stem):
  प्रथमा: मत्स्यः (ekavacana) / मत्स्यौ (dvivacana) / मत्स्याः (bahuvacana).
  द्वितीया: मत्स्यम् / मत्स्यौ / मत्स्यान्.
Notice त्रयः मत्स्याः ('three fishes') is प्रथमा बहुवचन, the subject; मत्स्यान् (in 'एतान् मत्स्यान् ग्रहीष्यामः') is द्वितीया बहुवचन, the object.

(D) धातुरूप — a few verbs from the lesson:
  • √एध् (to thrive, Atmanepada) present लट्: एधते / एधेते / एधन्ते. The verse-form एधेते is दुविवचन ('the two thrive').
  • √नश् (to perish) present: नश्यति; with prefix वि- → विनश्यति ('perishes').
  • √भू (to be/become) future लृट्: भविष्यति ('will be'); present भवति. यद्भविष्यः is built from यद् + भविष्य ('what-will-be').

सारांश — Summary

In this chapter you read the famous Panchatantra/Hitopadesha fable of the THREE FISHES. अनागतविधाता (foresight) left the dangerous lake in good time and was safe; प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः (presence of mind) was caught but cleverly played dead and escaped; and यद्भविष्यः (blind fatalist) trusted only to fate, made no effort, and perished. You learned the शब्दार्थ and translation of the tale, its moral — that foresight and presence of mind protect us while lazy fatalism destroys us — and the famous framing verse "अनागतविधाता च प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिस्तथा…". From the text you also studied सन्धि (यण्, नञ्, व्यञ्जन), the six विभक्ति with examples, the शब्दरूप of मत्स्य, and the धातुरूप of √एध्, √नश् and √भू. Remember the verse — it captures a whole philosophy of wise, active living in two lines.

topics.name: कथा-परिचयः — The Fable and its Source
topics.description: What the title यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति means, and the origin of the three-fishes story in the नीति-कथा tradition of the पञ्चतन्त्रम् (Panchatantra) and हितोपदेशः (Hitopadesha).

topics.name: त्रयः मत्स्याः — The Three Fishes and their Natures
topics.description: The three fishes and the meaning of their names: अनागतविधाता (foresight/fore-planner), प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः (presence of mind/ready-wit) and यद्भविष्यः (the fatalist, 'What-will-be'), and how each name captures a temperament.

topics.name: कथासारः — The Story Narrated
topics.description: The sequence of the tale in simple Sanskrit prose with शब्दार्थ and translation: the fishermen's plan, the escape of the fore-planner, the clever escape of the ready-wit, and the death of the fatalist.

topics.name: सन्देशः — Moral: Foresight and Presence of Mind vs Fatalism
topics.description: The moral of the story — that दूरदर्शिता (foresight) and प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः (presence of mind) with पुरुषार्थ (effort) save us, while blind दैववाद/भाग्यवाद (fatalism) and आलस्य (laziness) lead to ruin.

topics.name: श्लोकः — The Framing Verse
topics.description: The famous public-domain verse 'अनागतविधाता च प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिस्तथा। द्वावेतौ सुखमेधेते यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति॥', its word meanings and how it states the whole moral in two lines.

topics.name: व्याकरणम् — Grammar from the Lesson
topics.description: Grammar drawn from the text: सन्धि (यण्, नञ्, व्यञ्जन) with सन्धि-विच्छेद, the six विभक्ति case endings, the शब्दरूप of the a-stem मत्स्य, and the धातुरूप of √एध्, √नश् and √भू.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: कथा-परिचयः — The Fable and its Source
learning_outcomes.description: Explain the meaning of the title 'यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति' and identify the source of the three-fishes fable in the Panchatantra/Hitopadesha नीति-कथा tradition.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: त्रयः मत्स्याः — The Three Fishes and their Natures
learning_outcomes.description: Recall the names of the three fishes and state the meaning and temperament that each name (अनागतविधाता, प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः, यद्भविष्यः) represents.
Narrate the sequence of the story — the fishermen's plan, the fore-planner's departure, the ready-wit's clever escape, and the fatalist's death — in the correct order.
Give the शब्दार्थ (word meaning) in English of Sanskrit words drawn from the tale and use the vocabulary correctly.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: सन्देशः — Moral: Foresight and Presence of Mind vs Fatalism
learning_outcomes.description: Analyse the moral of the fable — foresight and presence of mind with effort save us, blind fatalism destroys us — and apply the lesson to everyday situations.
Identify and perform simple सन्धि joins and splits (यण्, नञ्, व्यञ्जन) using examples taken from the lesson.
Recognise the six विभक्ति case endings, the शब्दरूप of the a-stem मत्स्य and simple धातुरूप, and state the case/number/verb-form of a word from the text.
Translate the framing verse and lines of the tale into simple English and answer comprehension questions about words, grammar and moral.

chapter_summary.title: यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति (Yadbhavisyo Vinasyati) — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Secondary Sanskrit (209) summary for Chapter 6. It retells the famous Panchatantra/Hitopadesha fable of the three fishes, explains the moral that foresight and presence of mind save us while blind fatalism destroys us, studies the framing verse, and draws simple grammar from the tale.

branches.label: कथा — Story
details: Fishermen plan to net the fish 'tomorrow'
Fore-planner leaves at once, is safe

sections.heading: The fable and its source
bullets: यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति means 'the one called What-will-be perishes' — the punch-line of the three-fishes fable.
It is a नीति-कथा (moral animal fable) from the पञ्चतन्त्रम् and हितोपदेशः, works written to teach practical wisdom to the young.
In such tales, animals speak and act like people so that a moral can be taught in a delightful, memorable way.

sections.heading: The three fishes and their names
bullets: अनागतविधाता = 'one who plans for what has not yet come' — foresight (अनागत = future + विधाता = planner).
प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः = 'one whose wit arises on the spot' — presence of mind, ready intelligence.
यद्भविष्यः = 'What-will-be' — the fatalist who leaves everything to fate and makes no effort.
The names ARE the lesson: each names the quality (or fault) that decides the fish's fate.

sections.heading: What happens in the story
bullets: Fishermen see the plump fish and plan to net them all the next morning.
अनागतविधाता overhears, and at once swims by the water-channel to another safe lake — foresight.
प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः is caught, but floats motionless as if dead; thrown out as 'dead', he darts back and escapes — presence of mind.
यद्भविष्यः trusts only to fate, makes no effort, is caught and killed.

sections.heading: The moral (सन्देशः)
bullets: Foresight (दूरदर्शिता) — acting before trouble strikes — keeps us safe.
Presence of mind (प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः) — a cool, quick device in crisis — can save us even in danger.
Blind fatalism (दैववाद) plus laziness (आलस्य) leads to ruin; effort (पुरुषार्थ) must be joined to intelligence.
'Whatever will be, will be' must never become an excuse for doing nothing.

sections.heading: Grammar from the lesson
bullets: यण्-सन्धि: प्रति + उत्पन्नः = प्रत्युत्पन्नः (इ before उ → य्).
नञ्-सन्धि: न + आगतः = अनागतः ('not come' = future).
विभक्ति: जलाशये (locative 'in the lake'), जालेन (instrumental 'by the net'), मत्स्यान् (accusative plural 'the fishes').
शब्दरूप मत्स्य: मत्स्यः/मत्स्यौ/मत्स्याः; धातु एधेते (√एध्, dual 'thrive'), विनश्यति (√नश् 'perishes').

key_takeaways: यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति — 'the fatalist perishes' — is the moral of the Panchatantra/Hitopadesha three-fishes fable.
अनागतविधाता (foresight) leaves the dangerous lake in time and is completely safe.
प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः (presence of mind) is caught but plays dead and cleverly escapes.
यद्भविष्यः trusts only to fate, makes no effort, and is caught and killed.
The verse 'अनागतविधाता च प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिस्तथा। द्वावेतौ सुखमेधेते यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति॥' states the whole moral in two lines.
Wisdom is to join effort (पुरुषार्थ) to foresight and quick thinking, never to hide laziness behind 'whatever will be, will be'.
From the tale we learn सन्धि (प्रत्युत्पन्न, अनागत), the विभक्ति, the शब्दरूप of मत्स्य and the धातु √एध्/√नश्/√भू.

glossary.definition: 'What-will-be'; the name of the fatalist fish who leaves all to fate and perishes; from यद् (what) + भविष्यः (will be).
'One who plans for the future'; the fish with foresight (अनागत = not-yet-come + विधाता = arranger/planner).
'One whose wit arises on the spot'; presence of mind, ready intelligence in a crisis.
A fish; the a-stem masculine noun used as the शब्दरूप model in this lesson (मत्स्यः/मत्स्यौ/मत्स्याः).
A fisherman; the fishermen (धीवराः) who plan to net the fish in the tale.
A net; the instrument (जालेन, 'by the net') with which the fishermen catch the fish.
A lake or pond; the place (locative जलाशये, 'in the lake') where the three fishes live.
A moral fable, usually about animals, told to teach practical wisdom (नीति); the genre of the Panchatantra and Hitopadesha.
The famous ancient Sanskrit collection of नीति animal fables in which the three-fishes story appears.
Foresight; thinking ahead and acting before trouble comes, the quality of अनागतविधाता.
Fatalism; the belief that fate alone decides everything, which (when blind and lazy) ruins यद्भविष्यः.
Human effort/endeavour; the active striving that a wise person joins to intelligence instead of leaving all to fate.
'The two thrive/prosper'; dual present of the धातु √एध् ('to grow, thrive'), used in the framing verse.
'Perishes, is destroyed'; present of वि + √नश्, the verb applied to the fatalist यद्भविष्यः.
The splitting of a joined sandhi form back into its parts, e.g. प्रत्युत्पन्न = प्रति + उत्पन्न.

questions.question: What does the title 'यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति' mean, and from which famous collection of fables does this story come?
questions.answer: It means 'the one (called) Yad-bhavisya — What-will-be — perishes/is destroyed'. The story of the three fishes comes from the ancient Sanskrit नीति-कथा collections, the पञ्चतन्त्रम् (Panchatantra) and हितोपदेशः (Hitopadesha).
questions.explanation: Title meaning + source of the fable.

questions.question: Name the three fishes and give the meaning of each name in one phrase.
questions.answer: अनागतविधाता = 'one who plans for the future' (foresight); प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः = 'one whose wit arises on the spot' (presence of mind); यद्भविष्यः = 'What-will-be' (the fatalist).

questions.question: How did अनागतविधाता save himself? What quality did he show?
questions.answer: On overhearing the fishermen's plan to net the fish the next morning, अनागतविधाता at once left the lake by the water-channel and swam to another safe lake, escaping before the danger arrived. He showed दूरदर्शिता (foresight) — acting before trouble strikes.

questions.question: How did प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः escape after being caught in the net?
questions.answer: When caught in the net, प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः instantly thought of a device: he floated motionless as if dead. The fishermen, thinking him already dead, threw him out of the net; he at once darted back into the water and escaped. This was his presence of mind (प्रत्युत्पन्ना मतिः).
questions.explanation: Presence of mind: plays dead, escapes.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ (English meaning) of: धीवरः, जालम्, श्वः, विनष्टः.
questions.answer: धीवरः = fisherman; जालम् = net; श्वः = tomorrow; विनष्टः = destroyed/perished.

questions.question: Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद (split): (a) प्रत्युत्पन्नः (b) अनागतः.
questions.answer: (a) प्रत्युत्पन्नः = प्रति + उत्पन्नः (यण्-सन्धि: इ before उ → य्). (b) अनागतः = न + आगतः (नञ्-सन्धि: न → अन् before a vowel).
questions.explanation: Sandhi splitting from the two fish-names.

questions.question: State the विभक्ति (case) and its sense for each: जलाशये, जालेन, मत्स्यान्.
questions.answer: जलाशये = सप्तमी (locative) → 'in the lake'. जालेन = तृतीया (instrumental) → 'by the net'. मत्स्यान् = द्वितीया बहुवचन (accusative plural) → 'the fishes' (as object).

questions.question: Explain the moral of 'यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति' using the fates of the three fishes, and tell how a student can apply it today.
questions.answer:
The fable contrasts three attitudes. अनागतविधाता uses foresight (दूरदर्शिता): he acts before danger comes and is completely safe. प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः uses presence of mind: even after being caught he thinks of a clever device (playing dead) and escapes. But यद्भविष्यः trusts only to fate, saying 'whatever will be, will be', makes no effort, and is caught and killed. The moral is that foresight and quick, cool thinking — joined with effort (पुरुषार्थ) — protect us, while blind fatalism and laziness (आलस्य) destroy us.
A student applies this by preparing for exams well in advance (foresight), staying calm and thinking clearly when an unexpected problem arises (presence of mind), and never using 'whatever happens, happens' as an excuse to avoid work. Effort and planning, not blind luck, decide success.
questions.explanation: Moral through the three fishes + practical application.

questions.question: Write the framing verse 'अनागतविधाता च...' in Devanagari, give the शब्दार्थ of 'एधेते' and 'विनश्यति', and translate the verse.
questions.answer:
अनागतविधाता च प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिस्तथा। द्वावेतौ सुखमेधेते यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति॥
शब्दार्थ: एधेते = '(the two) thrive/prosper' (dual present of √एध्); विनश्यति = 'perishes, is destroyed' (वि + √नश्).
Translation: 'The fore-planner (अनागतविधाता) and likewise the ready-witted one (प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः) — these two thrive happily; but What-will-be (यद्भविष्यः, the fatalist) perishes.'

What does 'यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति' mean, and what kind of story is it?
questions.answer: It means 'the one called Yad-bhavisya (What-will-be) perishes'. It is a नीति-कथा — a moral animal fable (from the Panchatantra/Hitopadesha) that teaches practical wisdom.

questions.question: Why are stories like this one told with talking animals?
questions.answer: Animal fables (नीति-कथा) let a moral be taught in a short, delightful and memorable way. Children enjoy the talking fish and easily remember the lesson about foresight, quick wit and fatalism.

questions.question: Give the meaning of the name 'अनागतविधाता'.
questions.answer: अनागतविधाता means 'one who makes arrangements for what has not yet come' — that is, one who plans for the future. अनागत = not-yet-come (future); विधाता = arranger/planner. It stands for foresight.

questions.question: Give the meaning of the name 'प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः'.
questions.answer: प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः means 'one whose intelligence (मति) arises on the spot (प्रत्युत्पन्न)'. It stands for presence of mind — ready wit in a moment of crisis.

questions.question: Explain how the three names of the fishes match their fates.
questions.answer: अनागतविधाता ('fore-planner') uses foresight and is safe; प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः ('ready-wit') uses presence of mind and escapes; यद्भविष्यः ('what-will-be') trusts blindly to fate, makes no effort, and perishes. Each name names the quality (or fault) that decides its owner's fate.

questions.question: Describe in order what the three fishes did after the fishermen's plan was overheard.
questions.answer: First, अनागतविधाता at once left the lake by the water-channel for a safe lake. Second, प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः stayed, deciding to act when danger actually came. Third, यद्भविष्यः laughed, said 'whatever will be, will be', and did nothing. Next morning the first was already safe, the second played dead and escaped, and the third was caught and killed.

questions.question: What plan did the fishermen make at the lake?
questions.answer: Seeing many plump fish, the fishermen decided that the next morning (श्वः प्रातः) they would come and catch all the fish with their net, and then they went home.

questions.question: Why can we say प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः truly showed presence of mind?
questions.answer: Even after being trapped in the net — a moment of great danger — he did not panic. On the spot he thought of a clever device: he floated motionless as if dead, so the fishermen threw him out as a dead fish; he then instantly darted back into the water. Thinking of and carrying out this trick at the crisis moment is exactly 'presence of mind'.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: जलाशयः, तीरम्, निश्चलः.
questions.answer: जलाशयः = lake/pond; तीरम् = bank/shore; निश्चलः = motionless.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: उपायः, अनर्थः, गृहीतः.
questions.answer: उपायः = means/device/plan; अनर्थः = misfortune/calamity; गृहीतः = caught/seized.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: प्रतिकारः, दूरदर्शिता, वृथा.
questions.answer: प्रतिकारः = remedy/counter-measure; दूरदर्शिता = foresight; वृथा = in vain/uselessly.

questions.answer: धीवराः जालेन मत्स्यान् गृह्णन्ति। — 'The fishermen catch the fishes with a net.' Here जालेन (instrumental) means 'by/with the net'.

questions.question: State and explain the moral of the fable.
questions.answer: The moral is 'यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति' — the blind fatalist perishes. Foresight (दूरदर्शिता), which acts before danger, and presence of mind (प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः), which finds a device in crisis, both save life; but leaving everything to fate with no effort (आलस्य, दैववाद) leads to ruin. Wisdom is to join effort and intelligence, not to worship fate blindly.

questions.question: Give one real-life example of foresight (like अनागतविधाता).
questions.answer: Preparing for an examination weeks in advance instead of the night before, or saving money and keeping an umbrella ready before the rainy season — acting to prevent trouble before it arrives — is foresight like अनागतविधाता.

questions.question: 'Since everything is fixed by fate, effort is useless.' Using the fable, judge this statement.
questions.answer: The fable rejects this statement. यद्भविष्यः held exactly this belief, made no effort, and was killed, while अनागतविधाता and प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः acted wisely and survived. The story shows that human effort (पुरुषार्थ) joined to foresight and quick thinking decides our safety; 'whatever will be, will be' is a lazy excuse, not wisdom. So the statement is wrong.

questions.question: Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of: (a) प्रत्युत्पन्नः (b) अनागतः.
questions.answer: (a) प्रत्युत्पन्नः = प्रति + उत्पन्नः (यण्-सन्धि: इ before उ → य्). (b) अनागतः = न + आगतः (नञ्-सन्धि: न → अन् before a vowel).

questions.question: Join by sandhi and name the rule: (a) सुखम् + एधेते (b) यद् + भविष्यः.
questions.answer: (a) सुखम् + एधेते = सुखमेधेते (म् joins the following vowel). (b) यद् + भविष्यः = यद्भविष्यः (व्यञ्जन-सन्धि; द् stays before भ).

questions.question: What is यण्-सन्धि? Give one example from this lesson.
questions.answer: In यण्-सन्धि, the vowels इ/उ/ऋ, when they meet a dissimilar vowel, change into the semivowels य्/व्/र्. Example: प्रति + उत्पन्नः = प्रत्युत्पन्नः (इ before उ becomes य्).

questions.question: State the विभक्ति and sense of: (a) जलाशये (b) धीवरैः.
questions.answer: (a) जलाशये = सप्तमी (locative) — 'in the lake'. (b) धीवरैः = तृतीया (instrumental) plural — 'by the fishermen'.

questions.question: Write the शब्दरूप of मत्स्य in प्रथमा विभक्ति (all three numbers).
questions.answer: प्रथमा: एकवचन मत्स्यः, द्विवचन मत्स्यौ, बहुवचन मत्स्याः.

questions.question: Translate into English: 'धीवराः जालेन मत्स्यान् अगृह्णन्'.
questions.answer: 'The fishermen caught the fishes with a net.' धीवराः = fishermen; जालेन = with a net; मत्स्यान् = the fishes (object); अगृह्णन् = caught.

questions.question: Translate the framing verse 'अनागतविधाता च प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिस्तथा। द्वावेतौ सुखमेधेते यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति॥'.
questions.answer: 'The fore-planner (अनागतविधाता) and, likewise, the ready-witted one (प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः) — these two thrive happily; but What-will-be (यद्भविष्यः, the fatalist) perishes.' The verse names all three fishes and states the whole moral.

questions.question: What is the story 'यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति' about, and why are such नीति-कथा important?
questions.answer:
The lesson retells the famous fable of the three fishes who lived in one lake. Their names — अनागतविधाता (foresight), प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः (presence of mind) and यद्भविष्यः (fatalism) — describe their natures. When fishermen plan to net them, the first escapes by leaving early, the second by cleverly playing dead, and the third, trusting only to fate, is caught and killed. The title 'यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति' ('the fatalist perishes') sums up the moral.
Such नीति-कथा (moral animal fables from the Panchatantra and Hitopadesha) are important because they teach practical wisdom and values — foresight, quick thinking, effort — in a short, delightful and memorable form. Children remember the talking fish and, with them, the lesson; and, being in simple Sanskrit, the tales also help learners build vocabulary and grammar.
questions.explanation: Summary of the tale + value of fables.

questions.question: Describe the three fishes, the meaning of their names, and the temperament each represents.
questions.answer: The three fishes are अनागतविधाता, प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः and यद्भविष्यः. (1) अनागतविधाता means 'one who arranges for what has not yet come' (अनागत = future, विधाता = planner); he represents दूरदर्शिता (foresight) — planning ahead and acting before danger. (2) प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः means 'one whose wit arises on the spot' (प्रत्युत्पन्न = present-moment, मति = intelligence); he represents presence of mind — thinking of a clever device at the very moment of crisis. (3) यद्भविष्यः means 'What-will-be'; he represents blind fatalism (दैववाद) — leaving everything to fate and making no effort. Thus the three names stand for foresight, quick wit and fatalism, and the story shows how each temperament leads to safety or ruin.

questions.question: Narrate the full story of the three fishes in your own words.
questions.answer: In a certain lake lived three fishes who were friends but different in nature: अनागतविधाता, प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः and यद्भविष्यः. One evening some fishermen came to the bank, saw the plump fish, and decided to return the next morning to catch them all with their net. अनागतविधाता overheard this and thought, 'A wise creature removes danger before it comes'; at once he swam away by the water-channel to another safe lake. प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः chose to stay, deciding to act only when danger actually struck. यद्भविष्यः laughed, saying 'whatever will be, will be; fate is supreme', and idly stayed. Next morning the fishermen cast their net. अनागतविधाता was already safe. प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः was caught, but floated motionless as if dead; the fishermen threw the 'dead' fish out, and he instantly darted back into the water and escaped. यद्भविष्यः, having made no effort, was caught and killed. Thus 'yad-bhavisya perishes'.

questions.question: List and explain at least eight important words (शब्दार्थ) from this lesson.
questions.answer: 1. मत्स्यः = fish. 2. धीवरः = fisherman. 3. जालम् = net. 4. जलाशयः = lake/pond. 5. श्वः = tomorrow. 6. उपायः = means/device. 7. भाग्यम् = fate. 8. अनर्थः = calamity/misfortune. 9. निश्चलः = motionless (as प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः lay). 10. गृहीतः = caught/seized. 11. हतः = killed. 12. दूरदर्शिता = foresight. These words together tell the whole tale: the fishermen (धीवराः) plan to catch the fish (मत्स्यान्) with a net (जालेन) in the lake (जलाशये); one uses a device (उपाय), while the fatalist, trusting fate (भाग्य), is caught and killed.

questions.question: Discuss the moral of the fable and how a student can apply foresight, presence of mind and effort in daily life.
questions.answer:
The moral is that foresight and presence of mind, joined to effort, protect us, while blind fatalism ruins us. अनागतविधाता is saved by foresight, प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः by presence of mind, and यद्भविष्यः is destroyed because he trusts fate and does nothing. The tale does not deny fate; it warns against using 'whatever will be, will be' as an excuse for laziness (आलस्य).
A student can apply this in three ways. Foresight: plan studies, revise well before exams, keep materials ready, and anticipate difficulties. Presence of mind: when an unexpected question or problem appears, stay calm, think clearly and find the best available solution instead of panicking. Effort (पुरुषार्थ): work steadily and take responsibility rather than blaming luck. A student who plans ahead like अनागतविधाता and keeps a cool head like प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः will succeed, while one who behaves like यद्भविष्यः will fail. Thus the ancient fable gives very modern, practical advice.

questions.question: Explain सन्धि and सन्धि-विच्छेद with four examples taken from this lesson.
questions.answer:
सन्धि is the euphonic joining/merging of sounds where two words meet; सन्धि-विच्छेद is splitting such a joined form back into its parts. Examples from the lesson:
1. प्रति + उत्पन्नः = प्रत्युत्पन्नः (यण्-सन्धि: इ before उ becomes य्).
2. न + आगतः = अनागतः (नञ्-सन्धि: न appears as अन् before a vowel).
3. सुखम् + एधेते = सुखमेधेते (म् joins the following vowel).
4. यद् + भविष्यः = यद्भविष्यः (व्यञ्जन-सन्धि; द् stays before भ).
Being able both to join (सन्धि) and to split (सन्धि-विच्छेद) is essential for reading Sanskrit correctly.

questions.question: Explain the six विभक्ति with one example each drawn from this lesson, using मत्स्य or story words.
questions.answer: 1. प्रथमा (nominative, subject): मत्स्यः 'the fish', धीवराः 'the fishermen'. 2. द्वितीया (accusative, object): मत्स्यान् 'the fishes' (as object of 'catch'). 3. तृतीया (instrumental, 'by/with'): जालेन 'by the net', धीवरैः 'by the fishermen'. 4. पञ्चमी (ablative, 'from'): जालात् 'from the net'. 5. षष्ठी (genitive, 'of'): जलाशयस्य 'of the lake'. 6. सप्तमी (locative, 'in/at'): जलाशये 'in the lake', जले 'in the water'. Recognising these endings tells us who does what to whom in a sentence.

questions.question: Take the framing verse, give the word meanings, translate it, and explain how it sums up the story.
questions.answer:
Verse: अनागतविधाता च प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिस्तथा। द्वावेतौ सुखमेधेते यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति॥
शब्दार्थ: अनागतविधाता = the fore-planner; च = and; प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः = the ready-witted one; तथा = likewise; द्वौ एतौ = these two; सुखम् = happily; एधेते = (the two) thrive; यद्भविष्यः = the fatalist; विनश्यति = perishes.
Translation: 'The fore-planner and, likewise, the ready-witted one — these two thrive happily; but What-will-be (the fatalist) perishes.'
The verse names all three fishes and states the entire moral in a single line: foresight and presence of mind bring well-being, while blind fatalism brings ruin. It is the perfect summary of the tale.
questions.explanation: Verse meaning + how it sums the story.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
कस्मिंश्चित् जलाशये त्रयः मत्स्याः वसन्ति स्म — अनागतविधाता, प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः, यद्भविष्यः च।
(a) कति मत्स्याः? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'जलाशये'. (c) In which विभक्ति is 'जलाशये'? (d) Name the three fishes.
questions.answer: (a) त्रयः (three) मत्स्याः. (b) जलाशये = 'in the lake'. (c) जलाशये is सप्तमी (locative). (d) The three are अनागतविधाता, प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः and यद्भविष्यः.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
धीवराः अवदन् — 'श्वः प्रातः वयम् आगत्य जालेन मत्स्यान् ग्रहीष्यामः।'
(a) Who is speaking? (b) When will they come? (c) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'जालेन'. (d) What is their plan?
questions.answer: (a) The धीवराः (fishermen) are speaking. (b) They will come the next morning (श्वः प्रातः). (c) जालेन = 'with a net'. (d) Their plan is to come next morning and catch all the fish with their net.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
अनागतविधाता तत् श्रुत्वा अचिन्तयत् — 'अनर्थः आगमिष्यति; अहम् अद्य एव अन्यत् सरः गच्छामि।' एवं सः जलमार्गेण अगच्छत्।
(a) What did अनागतविधाता decide? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'अनर्थः'. (c) By what route did he leave? (d) What quality did he show?
questions.answer: (a) He decided to leave the lake at once for another lake before the danger came. (b) अनर्थः = calamity/misfortune. (c) He left by the water-channel (जलमार्गेण). (d) He showed दूरदर्शिता (foresight).

questions.question:
Read and answer:
प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः जाले बद्धः अभवत्, किन्तु सः मृतवत् निश्चलः अभवत्। धीवराः तं मृतम् मत्वा बहिः अक्षिपन्, सः च पुनः जले प्रविश्य अपलायत।
(a) What happened to प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः first? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'निश्चलः'. (c) Why did the fishermen throw him out? (d) What quality does this show?
questions.answer: (a) He was first caught (बद्धः) in the net. (b) निश्चलः = motionless. (c) They thought he was dead (मृतम् मत्वा) and so threw him out. (d) It shows प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः — presence of mind.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
यद्भविष्यः अवदत् — 'यद् भविष्यति तद् भविष्यति; भाग्यम् एव प्रबलम्।' सः किमपि उपायम् न अकरोत्, अतः धीवरैः हतः।
(a) What did यद्भविष्यः believe? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'भाग्यम्'. (c) What did he do about the danger? (d) What was the result, and what is the lesson?
questions.answer: (a) He believed 'whatever will be, will be; fate alone is supreme'. (b) भाग्यम् = fate/destiny. (c) He did nothing (न उपायम् अकरोत्) about the danger. (d) He was caught and killed by the fishermen; the lesson is that blind fatalism with no effort leads to ruin.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer:
अनागतविधाता च प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिस्तथा।
द्वावेतौ सुखमेधेते यद्भविष्यो विनश्यति॥
(a) Which two thrive happily? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'एधेते'. (c) Who perishes? (d) State the moral of the verse.
questions.answer: (a) अनागतविधाता and प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः (the two) thrive happily. (b) एधेते = '(the two) thrive/prosper'. (c) यद्भविष्यः (the fatalist) perishes. (d) Moral: foresight and presence of mind bring well-being; blind fatalism brings ruin.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
The fishes' names contain sandhi: 'प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः' and 'अनागतविधाता'.
(a) Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of 'प्रत्युत्पन्नः'. (b) Name that sandhi. (c) Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of 'अनागतः'. (d) Name that sandhi.
questions.answer: (a) प्रत्युत्पन्नः = प्रति + उत्पन्नः. (b) यण्-सन्धि (इ before उ → य्). (c) अनागतः = न + आगतः. (d) नञ्-सन्धि (न → अन् before a vowel).

questions.question:
Read and answer:
धीवराः जालेन जलाशये मत्स्यान् अगृह्णन्।
(a) In which विभक्ति is 'धीवराः'? (b) In which विभक्ति is 'जालेन', and what is its sense? (c) In which विभक्ति is 'मत्स्यान्'? (d) In which विभक्ति is 'जलाशये'?
questions.answer: (a) धीवराः = प्रथमा (nominative) plural, the subject. (b) जालेन = तृतीया (instrumental) — 'by/with the net'. (c) मत्स्यान् = द्वितीया (accusative) plural, the object. (d) जलाशये = सप्तमी (locative) — 'in the lake'.
questions.explanation: Comprehension: four cases in one sentence.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
तेषां त्रयाणां मत्स्यानां स्वभावाः भिन्नाः आसन् — एकः दूरदर्शी, अपरः प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः, तृतीयः तु भाग्यवादी।
(a) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'स्वभावः'. (b) Who is 'दूरदर्शी'? (c) Who is 'भाग्यवादी'? (d) What quality does प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः stand for?
questions.answer: (a) स्वभावः = nature/temperament. (b) The far-sighted (दूरदर्शी) one is अनागतविधाता. (c) The fatalist (भाग्यवादी) is यद्भविष्यः. (d) प्रत्युत्पन्नमतिः stands for presence of mind (ready wit).

questions.question:
Read and answer:
बुद्धिमान् आपदः आगमनात् पूर्वम् एव प्रतिकारं करोति; यः भाग्ये एव विश्वसिति सः विनश्यति।
(a) When does a wise person act? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'प्रतिकारः'. (c) Who perishes, according to the sentence? (d) How can you apply this in your life?
questions.answer: (a) A wise person acts before the danger arrives (आगमनात् पूर्वम्). (b) प्रतिकारः = remedy/counter-measure. (c) One who trusts only in fate (भाग्ये एव विश्वसिति) perishes. (d) I can apply it by preparing early and taking timely action — for example studying ahead of exams — instead of leaving things to luck.
